book: 038 - Radiohead and Philosophy - Fitter Happier More Deductive

chapters.file: ch02 - Radiohead and Philosophy.md
ch03 - Radiohead and Philosophy.md
ch04 - Title Page.md
ch05 - 1 Step.md
chapters.relation: The editors' introduction argues that Radiohead succeeded The Clash as 'the only band that matters' partly for philosophical reasons: rather than stating abstractions, their music points toward analyses of our actual historical situation, showing 'how it should be possible for pop music to incarnate a particular historical situation' (Greif's question). It reads the laser-data 'House of Cards' video as proof that in our world only the underlying data matters, with Radiohead releasing the source code so fans can re-image it themselves. It then previews the volume's encounters: Heidegger's phenomenology and the manipulation of Yorke's voice on Kid A, Marx on the pay-what-you-want release of In Rainbows, and the pathos of Aristotelian tragedy running through the sad songs.

chapters.file: ch06 - Anyone Can Play Philosophy.md
ch07 - Where Pink Floyd Ends and Radiohead Begins.md
chapters.relation: Reisch asks whether Radiohead is the Pink Floyd of the twenty-first century and answers that the comparison misleads: where Barrett-era Floyd used electronics to escape into psychedelic fantasy, Radiohead's apparent space-rock is phenomenological, giving voice to pre-reflective experience of technological modern life. He reads 'No Surprises' (Yorke singing with his head in a filling glass sphere) as a study in the political infantilization of commuters, and OK Computer's car crash ('Airbag'), 'Let Down', and 'Lucky' as registering the feel of a fragile, technology-saturated world. Quoting Marcuse's One-Dimensional Man and Chomsky on manufactured consent, he argues we can see no alternative to the technologically rational system, and then, against Descartes' priority of the isolated 'I', invokes Heidegger's Being-in-the-world and Merleau-Ponty's embodied subject to suggest that our deepening immersion in technology may be changing the self itself — the truth the collapsing pedestrians of the 'Just' video cannot face.

chapters.file: ch08 - 2. - Radiohead, or the Philosophy of Pop.md
chapters.relation: Greif asks how pop music could ever 'incarnate a particular historical situation' and answers with Radiohead's portrait of broadcast culture around 2000: an environing, objectless dread in which each person lives at a knot of shouted messages no one sent and complaining only marks you as a crank. The band's turn to electronica was not avant-garde innovation but the discovery of the sound of that second nature, with Yorke's sampled-and-broken voice alternately absorbed into the machine and reasserting the human, and the lyric 'we' sliding between a scared individual lying that he is not alone, a wished-for collectivity, and the ventriloquized tyrant (as with Brecht's Pirate Jenny). Radiohead's church-tinged sublimity observes the storm from inside it — an internalized, inhuman sublime rather than the tradition's safe vantage on crushing power. Pop, he concludes, neither mirrors us nor preaches: it lets us retain and reactivate knowledge social speech forbids, and its deepest effect is not revolution but defiance — the retention of a private voice, a politics of re-created privacy — epitomized by 'There There' warning 'just 'cause you feel it doesn't mean it's there' inside an art form devoted to making you feel.

chapters.file: ch09 - You’re Living in a Fantasy World, This Beautiful World.md
chapters.relation: Sylvia argues that the split-screen 'All I Need' video made for MTV's anti-trafficking EXIT project — an American child's comfortable day intercut with a child laborer finishing the very shoes the American takes off — argues against child labor more powerfully than a standard utilitarian argument, because it joins Aristotle's ethos, pathos, and logos instead of relying on logos alone. Using the cognitive/expressive distinction, he claims the song also argues by turning listeners back on themselves ('I only stick with you because there are no others'). He then deploys Nozick's experience machine: we are all plugged into a Baudrillardian, Matrix-like media hyperreality that can make exploitation fade into background images, and the video's slap in the face 'punctures the hyperreality', showing how emotion can do argumentative work that rigorous argument cannot.

chapters.file: ch10 - Are Musical Experiences Universal.md
chapters.relation: Slowik uses Radiohead's evolution — from the standard pop structures of Pablo Honey and The Bends to the layered, quasi-classical textures of Kid A and Amnesiac ('In Limbo''s independent melodic lines, the wordless climax of 'Pyramid Song') — to introduce the philosophy of music. He weighs what a musical work is, testing nominalism, idealism, and realism against 'Like Spinning Plates' and its live versions, then pits the emotion theory against formalism in explaining how songs like 'Like Spinning Plates' move us. The chapter closes on whether musical experience is universal and on Hume's 'Standard of Taste': if the test of time validates greatness, then the argument over whether OK Computer or In Rainbows is the better album might actually have an objectively right answer.

chapters.file: ch11 - Art and Belief.md
ch12 - Rise and Shine It’s On Again Off Again.md
chapters.relation: Surber proposes Kristeva's 'abject aesthetics' as the new pair of shades that makes Radiohead legible: 'Creep' expresses abjection (the creep excluded even from recognition by the beautiful people), the android of 'Paranoid Android' is a borderline phenomenon neither human nor machine, and the bodily imagery of 'Bones', 'My Iron Lung', and the corpse in 'Knives Out' enacts the eruption of the pre-linguistic, formless abject, as do Donwood's dissolving Kid A letters. He contrasts the Beatles' aesthetics of psychedelic transcendence and Pink Floyd's existentialist aesthetics of alienation — built on Sartre's 'Hell is other people' gaze and the being-for-itself/being-in-itself split — with Radiohead's fluid, boundary-less world where meanings never come into focus and no existential revolt is possible because the embodied self is part of the world. Against the charge of nihilism, he reads Hail to the Thief and In Rainbows ('How come I end up where I started?') as postmodern reconstruction: if boundaries and meanings are fluid, they can also be remade.

chapters.file: ch13 - Where Tragedy Ends and Community Begins.md
chapters.relation: Lott takes up Augustine's puzzle about why we enjoy watching sufferings we would flee, and answers for Radiohead with Aristotle's theory of tragedy: songs like 'Karma Police', 'Exit Music', and 'Fake Plastic Trees' sketch fragmentary characters in breakdown whose undeserved yet partly self-inflicted sufferings — 'Just'''s 'you do it to yourself' is hamartia — evoke pity and fear and then catharsis. Singing along makes identification uniquely intense in pop ('for a minute there, I lost myself' blurs the listener into the character), while music's 'natural sweetness' and its dynamics of build, climax, and release carry the purgation, from the terror of 'Climbing Up the Walls' to the slow ache of 'Videotape'. Because tragedy, unlike history, deals in universals, songs like 'The Bends' and 'High and Dry' open onto reflection on happiness, vulnerability, and the culture that fosters isolation, ending in the thin but real community of listeners who recognize their shared fragility.

chapters.file: ch14 - There Are No Unrelated Phenomena.md
chapters.relation: Dark reads Thom Yorke's solo album The Eraser as an experiment in bearing witness — from Donwood's King Canute 'Gold Cnut' cover to 'Harrowdown Hill', which eulogizes David Kelly, the UN weapons inspector whose inconvenient fact-checking of the Iraq WMD dossier preceded his death ('we think the same things at the same time / we just can't do anything about it'). Drawing on Derrida — religion is responsibility or nothing, a poem is nothing without the risk of meaninglessness, words remain under erasure — he argues that Yorke's pub-table 'collating information' ('Analyze', 'And It Rained All Night'''s 'a million engines in neutral') is a sacred, self-undermining act of attention against officialdom's insistence that this has nothing to do with that. Camus's line that crushing truths perish from being acknowledged frames the witness, and the chapter closes by hearing 'Reckoner' ('dedicated to all human beings') as the communal fulfillment of that witness.

chapters.file: ch15 - Radiohead and the Music Industry.md
ch16 - This Is Really Happening (So Do Something).md
chapters.relation: Milsky argues that Radiohead practice what environmental virtue ethics preaches, organizing the chapter around Aristotle's akrasia (Nicomachean Ethics VII): Sting, who champions rainforests while advertising Jaguar and topping the 'dirtiest band' carbon table, acts against his own better judgment, whereas Radiohead — confronted with an audit showing their 2003 and 2006 tours emitted roughly 11,368 tons of CO2, mostly from fans driving — changed their actual practice (venues near public transit, car-pool lots, sea freight instead of air, LED lighting and auxilary power units). He reads the King Canute imagery of The Eraser and lines from 'The Clock' and 'And It Rained All Night' as environmental narrative in the tradition of Thoreau's Walden and Leopold's Sand County Almanac, obligating listeners to act or risk akrasia themselves, and presents the band's Friends of the Earth 'Big Ask' commitment as linking environmental virtue to human flourishing. 'Idioteque'''s 'this is really happening' becomes the wake-up call to the akratic fan driving to Lollapalooza with a bottled water.

chapters.file: ch17 - C-M-C Music Factory.md
chapters.relation: Tate reads Radiohead's career through Marx: the band's standing tension between what they would make of themselves and what their record company would make of them is the worker's plight, and 'We Suck Young Blood' — with its fake 'we want sweet meats' recruitment campaign — literalizes Marx's vampire imagery of capital that 'lives only by sucking living labour'. Yorke's documented unease about money, from the 'six fluffy wee rabbits' mock-interview to 'Meeting People Is Easy'''s confession that money gets a band 'by the balls', maps onto Marx's account of labour degraded into 'a fragment of a man', whose Amnesiac echo is 'Dollars and Cents''' 'we're going to crack your little souls'. The pay-what-you-want release of In Rainbows is then read as Marx's C-M-C circuit — selling music to live and make more music rather than M-C-M' accumulation for its own sake — a move that removes the exploitative capitalist middle-man instead of becoming one, and frees the band to make their most human-sounding album, fingers on strings.

chapters.file: ch18 - Go Slowly.md
chapters.relation: Wittkower frames In Rainbows' pay-what-you-want release with Adorno and Horkheimer's culture industry: music is expressive communication awkwardly trapped in commodity form — even 'Happy Birthday' has an owner until 2030 — and digital distribution is finally tearing that frame down. He then applies Rawls's justice as fairness to music distribution: the first principle now supports everyone's liberty to listen, rip, and share, because viable alternative models mean restricting listeners can no longer be justified as necessary to artists; and the difference principle, with the sadists-objection to utilitarian aggregation, shows that how benefits are distributed among persons matters, which he extends to racial wealth gaps and the affirmative-action dilemma. His conclusion is that we must 'go slowly': listeners' rights to their culture outweigh labels' legitimate profit expectations, the way emancipation outweighed plantation business models, and labels must adapt into service providers rather than gatekeepers.

chapters.file: ch19 - Radiohead’s Existential Politics.md
ch20 - Brush the Cobwebs from the Sky, Let the Genie Out from the Bottle.md
chapters.relation: Lougheed reads OK Computer, Kid A, and Amnesiac as portraits of Nietzsche's Last Humans: passive, resentful denizens of the world after the death of God, from the 'No Surprises' narrator begging for his quiet life of carbon monoxide to the 'Everything in Its Right Place' man sucking a lemon over the loss of objective right and wrong, whose isolated malice ('when I am king you will be first against the wall') is perspectivism collapsed into passive nihilism. Hail to the Thief then breaks from this landscape: its protagonists risk transcendence as Over Humans who create new, life-affirming values ('2 + 2 = 5'''s 'don't question my authority', 'Backdrifts''' 'nothing more to lose'), keep a critical distance from society's nihilistic sickness ('Where I End and You Begin'), and test their lives against eternal recurrence ('Sail to the Moon'''s 'know right from wrong', '15 Step'''s ending up where you started). The chapter closes by weighing Nietzsche's over-human project against critics who prefer gradual, generational self-overcoming for everyone.

chapters.file: ch21 - How to Misunderstand Politics Completely.md
chapters.relation: Melançon argues Radiohead's real politics lie not in the overt content of Hail to the Thief but in a Camusian movement from absurdity to revolt: 'Exit Music'''s violent shift from Romeo's tender 'you' to the distorted 'we hope that you choke' enacts revolt against imposed rules and wisdom, while the android of 'Fitter Happier' ('a pig in a cage on antibiotics') and the wished-for alien of 'Subterranean Homesick Alien' dramatize absurd life under others' dictates. Following The Myth of Sisyphus and The Rebel — 'I revolt, therefore we are' — he shows how the songs' 'I' becomes a collective 'we' ('Karma Police', 'Lucky', 'Dollars and Cents') whose revolt, like Sisyphus's conscious walk back down the mountain, affirms life without ever justifying murder. Merleau-Ponty's philosophy of expression then explains why the songs are political anyway: artists express a still-unspoken 'fever' (it took years before 'Nude' could be said), creating a public and a common world — politics as unveiling rather than governing, down to 'Electioneering'''s admission that the band too campaigns for our vote.

holes.name: Julia Kristeva
holes.what: French-Bulgarian psychoanalytic theorist whose The Powers of Horror (1980) introduced 'the abject' — what the clean subject expels (corpses, bodily fluids, the formless) — as a psychical and aesthetic category.
holes.why: Chapter 12's entire reading of 'Creep', the Kid A artwork, and Radiohead's boundary-dissolving songs is built on Kristeva and her book, which the taxonomy lacks.

holes.name: The Abject (abjection)
holes.what: Kristeva's notion of what is 'cast off' from the ordered world of subjects and objects — the bodily, formless, borderline — which simultaneously repels and fascinates, grounding an 'abject aesthetics'.
holes.why: Chapter 12 uses abjection as the master aesthetic category for Radiohead's lyrics and imagery, and no existing slug (beautiful, sublime, authentic) covers it.

holes.name: Catharsis (tragic purgation of pity and fear)
holes.what: Aristotle's account in the Poetics and Politics that tragedy (and music) evokes pity and fear and then purges them, yielding tragedy's own proper pleasure.
holes.why: Chapter 13 explains the pleasure of Radiohead's sad songs entirely through Aristotelian catharsis, which no existing Aristotle slug in the taxonomy names.

holes.name: Ontology of Musical Works
holes.what: The debate over what kind of entity a musical work is — particular performances and scores (nominalism), a mental idea (idealism), or an abstract object like a number (realism).
holes.why: Chapter 10's core question 'What is music?' is exactly this ontology debate, tested on 'Like Spinning Plates' and 'Optimistic', for which the taxonomy has no concept.

holes.name: Expression and the Action of Culture
holes.what: Merleau-Ponty's view that artists (and politicians) express a still-unspoken 'fever' of experience, creating works that summon a public and make the world common — an 'action of culture' distinct from governing.
holes.why: Chapter 21's second half rests on this Merleau-Ponty account of artistic expression and politics-as-unveiling, while the taxonomy's only Merleau-Ponty entry is embodiment, which the chapter does not use.
